transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-15
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~1h12m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood CSM), Carlos (Halcyon Head Infra), Priya (Halcyon Sec Eng), Leah (Halcyon Compliance), Tom (Platform), Anya (Ops)

Optional auto sections (quick):
Summary: deep dive on on-prem network isolation options, KMS/HSM integration patterns, audit log flows to SIEM, and egress-lockdown patterns for SOC 2 readiness. Action items and follow ups captured.
Topics: VPC hornets: egress, NAT, private endpoints; KMS/HSM connectivity (offline vs VPC endpoint); audit logs and SIEM ingestion; RBAC and SSO; certs and mTLS between services; model updates in air-gapped environment.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll do a quick intros and then jump into the onprem and kms stuff. Maya and I are from Redwood, Maya'll run the technical bits.
[00:12] Carlos: thanks. quick note, we've got several folks on, and it's fine if we go deep — Priya is our sec lead.
[00:20] Priya: hi all, yep, we'll focus on isolation, egress, and how keys are handled. also SOC 2 requirements and chain of custody.
[00:28] Maya: great. before we start, what is your current topology? do you have a single VPC with a dedicated subnet for inference, or are you planning physical racks?
[00:36] Tom: we have two datacenters, primary colo and a DR colo, both run k8s clusters for inference on baremetal. the plan is to run Redwood Private in their own VLAN/rack per site.
[00:45] Jordan: perfect, so talk to me about egress — do you currently allow outbound to public internet from the inference racks?
[00:52] Anya: minimal egress. most of our services go through a proxy and egress is restricted to a firewall allow-list. model downloads today are done via a controlled jump-host into a staging network.
[01:03] Maya: ok that lines up with a common pattern. for Redwood Private we usually see three integration modes for key management: 1) VPC endpoint to a cloud KMS (if in cloud), 2) HSM over private peering / dedicated link, 3) an on-prem HSM with a sidecar that talks to a local KMS. which of those are you leaning to?
[01:22] Priya: HSM on-prem is preferred — our compliance requires key custody. but we need to understand how Redwood's runtime will authenticate without opening broad egress.
[01:31] Maya: understood. options: mutual TLS pinned to a client cert provisioned into the HSM, or an intermediate key broker inside your network that has a VPC endpoint to Redwood control-plane. we can also support an offline-signed token flow for air-gapped model pulls.
[01:46] Leah: when you say control-plane, are we talking about any data leaving our network? SOC 2 wants to see no PHI leaves unencrypted and we need to be able to audit access.
[01:55] Jordan: short answer: model payloads and inference inputs can be configured to never leave the private network for Private deployment. control-plane telemetry and metrics can be routed via a customer-managed telemetry forwarder — we don't need raw logs by default.
[02:07] Carlos: how do you handle audit logs? we need immutable audit logs for both infra access and model-serving events, and those need to go to our SIEM (Splunk).
[02:14] Maya: Redwood can emit structured audit events locally and forward them to a syslog/HTTPS endpoint, or ship via an agent to your SIEM over an internal network path. we also support signed event logs — basically append-only log files with rotation and HMAC, or integration with your existing HSM for log signing.
[02:30] Priya: is that HMAC signing separate from KMS keys? we want the signing key in an HSM.
[02:36] Maya: yes, you can keep the signing key in the HSM. Redwood's agent will call the HSM via PKCS#11 or KMIP depending on your HSM vendor. note: PKCS#11 requires local library access, KMIP can run over TLS. both supported.
[02:50] Tom: any special firewall rules needed between the inference nodes and the HSM? our HSM sits on a management VLAN with strict ACLs.
[02:57] Maya: typically allow limited outbound on the HSM management ports (e.g., KMIP 5696 or vendor port) from the agent host. If using a sidecar model, the sidecar runs co-located with the inference process and the network policy can be namespace-restricted.
[03:10] Carlos: we prefer no direct internet egress — everything goes via a NAT in our mgmt VPC, and any external egress is via a proxy with TLS interception. will that break mutual TLS to the HSM?
[03:19] Maya: TLS interception is tricky — it interferes with mTLS to HSM. we recommend bypassing the proxy for HSM endpoints, put an explicit allow rule in the proxy for HSM IPs, or use a dedicated peering link.
[03:30] Priya: for SOC 2 we also need RBAC and SSO. how does Redwood map SAML roles to runtime permissions?
[03:36] Jordan: we integrate with SAML/SSO providers, and map groups to RBAC roles in the Redwood Console. for Private installs we can configure an on-prem identity connector. the important bit is token expiration and refresh lifecycle — we support short-lived tokens and revocation endpoints.
[03:49] Leah: can we push logs of admin role changes to our audit collector?
[03:54] Evan: yes, admin events (role changes, API key creation, key rotation) are emitted as audit events. we can route them to your collector over a secure channel. we recommend TLS with client certs for authentication.
[04:06] Maya: a note on network-level controls — policy options we usually suggest: 1) physical/rack separation, 2) VLAN segmentation per environment, 3) k8s network policies with egress deny-by-default, 4) host-based firewall for double enforcement.
[04:20] Tom: we use Calico with egress policies and L3 isolation, but we haven't enforced deny-by-default across every namespace yet. what's the risk?
[04:28] Maya: low risk if your workloads are well-scoped, but for SOC 2, deny-by-default with explicit allow lists is cleaner for audits. it reduces blast radius. also consider eBPF based policies for micro egress control if you need per-process granularity.
[04:44] Priya: ok, what about software updates for models — we need chain-of-custody for model bits, since some models are customer-provided.
[04:51] Maya: pattern: sign artifacts on your build host using your HSM, store checksum/manifest in an internal artifact registry accessible only over private network, and have an offline verifier on the inference host that validates signatures before load. Redwood's runtime supports signature verification hooks.
[05:03] Carlos: that implies some storage local to the inference cluster?
[05:07] Maya: yes, a private artifact registry or NFS with restricted mounts. or use a USB-based airgap artefact with manual transfer — Redwood supports an install flow for offline models.
[05:16] Leah: any encryption-in-use features for model state (KV caches)? are they resident in memory or swap?
[05:21] Maya: KV cache is in memory by default, ephemeral. for persistence we support encrypted checkpointing to disk with LUKS or filesystem-level encryption and you can encrypt the keys with your KMS. we also offer an option to encrypt cache in memory with process-level encryption, though that's heavier.
[05:36] Jordan: just to jump in, customers sometimes worry about swap and crash dumps. we recommend turning off swap on inference hosts and configuring kernel core_pattern so dumps are disabled or redirected to a protected collector.
[05:47] Anya: question: how does Redwood handle fallback to hosted models? if Private capacity is saturated, do requests ever leave the private network?
[05:54] Maya: fallback can be configured — we support strict offline-only mode (no external fallback) or fallthrough to a designated fallback model inside a customer-managed network path. by default we do not route customer data to Redwood-hosted endpoints for Private deployments unless explicitly configured.
[06:08] Priya: good. can we get a diagram that shows network flows for three modes — full air-gapped, HSM peering, and proxy-with-limited-egress?
[06:15] Jordan: yes, we'll attach a diagram. Maya will draft one showing ports and allowed CIDRs.
[06:20] [06:20] Jordan: moving on to SIEM integration. what format do you want? syslog over TLS, HTTP(S) JSON events, or direct Splunk forwarder?
[06:29] Carlos: Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC) is our standard. it's internal-only.
[06:33] Maya: we can post JSON events to HEC over mTLS. events are structured with a schema — user, action, resource, outcome, timestamp, and signed_event_id. we recommend sending both raw and enriched events as required.
[06:46] Priya: any latency concerns when emitting audit events synchronously? we don't want blocking in the critical path.
[06:52] Maya: audit events should be async. Redwood buffers and retries on failure. critical admin actions can be configured to wait for confirmation, but not inference-level logs.
[06:59] Tom: about firewalling, what's the recommended pattern between inference nodes and storage for model shards?
[07:05] Maya: use private subnets with security groups allowing only relevant ports, put storage behind VPC endpoints or VLAN ACLs, and ensure the storage endpoints are only reachable from the inference subnet. use mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic where possible.
[07:17] Leah: for compliance we need evidence of key rotation. how does Redwood surface key-rotation events?
[07:23] Evan: key rotation events are logged as audit records and can be exported to your SIEM. we also produce rotation reports — rotation timestamp, key id, rotated-by, and associated signature.
[07:34] Carlos: small aside — are there any third-party dependencies in the runtime that would break FIPS requirements?
[07:40] Maya: we have a FIPS-140 compatible crypto path for common operations. some optional acceleration paths (vendor-specific) may not be FIPS certified; we can provide a FIPS-compatible build for Private installs if you need it.
[07:53] Priya: about RBAC scoping — can you restrict model access per-team and tie that to SAML groups? we want analysts not to invoke certain models.
[07:59] Jordan: yes, per-route and per-model permissions map to SAML groups. we can enforce policy at the token level so tokens issued for analysts lack permission to call restricted models.
[08:09] Anya: do you support conditional access — like IP or device-based?
[08:13] Jordan: for the control plane yes, you can enforce device certs and IP allow lists for admin UI. runtime calls use client credentials and least-privilege tokens.
[08:21] Tom: curious on TLS client cert handling for mTLS — do you use short lived certs or long lived?
[08:26] Maya: short lived is best — rotate frequently with an automated rotation agent. long lived certs are acceptable for hardware-bound identities in HSM, but prefer short burst tokens for services.
[08:36] Priya: ok, can you explain the offline-signed token flow again? I think I missed a bit earlier.
[08:41] Maya: sure. workflow: you sign a request payload or an access token with a private key that lives inside your HSM. the runtime verifies the signature locally before accepting the model or request. no need for outbound calls during verification. that covers air-gapped scenarios.
[08:56] Carlos: about ingress — do you support SNI-based routing and TLS termination at the edge? we prefer termination at a reverse proxy for inspection.
[09:03] Maya: we support both. you can terminate TLS at your edge proxy and then use mTLS to backend, or have the runtime terminate TLS directly. for inspection, termination at the edge is common. ensure certs are rotated and access to private keys is audited.
[09:16] Leah: any notes on data residency? we have EU customers and need data to stay in EU.
[09:21] Jordan: for Private you deploy in-site or in your cloud region; data residency is an operational constraint. we support region pinning and will not move data across regions unless configured.
[09:29] Priya: one more: do you ever cache customer tokens or PII in logs?
[09:34] Maya: we redact PII and tokens by default from logs. you can configure stricter redaction policies. raw payloads are not stored unless you opt in for debug, which is gated and logged.
[09:44] Anya: what about LDAPS / AD integration for SSO? we use AD on-prem with LDAPS and need group sync.
[09:50] Jordan: we support LDAP/AD connectors and group sync. for on-prem deployments the connector runs inside your network and only talks to your AD over LDAPS. sync intervals can be tuned.
[09:59] Carlos: ok can we talk about network zoning for the rack? e.g., management network, inference network, model staging, and admin VLAN. how do you recommend we split?
[10:07] Maya: common split: management VLAN (for HSM, monitoring), admin VLAN (bastions, jump hosts), inference VLAN (GPU hosts), staging VLAN (artifact ingestion). enforce ACLs between them: management-only to staging for artifact transfer, inference-only to storage for model load, and admin to all for ops. no direct path from public internet to inference VLAN.
[10:27] Priya: do you have a recommended bastion pattern? we have strict access via bastion with MFA.
[10:32] Jordan: bastion -> ephemeral jump credentials -> audited session manager. we recommend session recording and just-in-time access. you can integrate with your SSO to provision ephemeral session tokens.
[10:42] Leah: any vendor certs or attestation we need to collect from Redwood for SOC 2?
[10:47] Evan: we can provide SOC 2 Type II coverage for our hosted services; for Private we provide a compliance artifacts pack that includes architecture diagrams, encryption details, and our internal SOC checklist. final attestation depends on deployment boundaries.
[10:59] Carlos: can Redwood be included in our penetration tests for Private? we need to run an internal red team on the deployed runtime.
[11:05] Maya: yes, we allow penetration testing on Private installs under a coordinated schedule and NDA. we ask for a vulnerability disclosure window and request you to share findings so we can patch.
[11:12] Priya: are there any default open ports in the runtime we should be aware of?
[11:17] Maya: default: health port on 8081 (configurable), admin gRPC endpoints only on loopback by default, and management ports for agent/HSM like KMIP. we'll provide a full ports list in the diagram.
[11:30] Tom: about egress hardening, do you support DNS whitelisting? we use DNS filtering extensively.
[11:36] Maya: yes, you can restrict domain resolution and use split-horizon DNS for internal endpoints. Redwood recommends using private DNS zones for internal artifact registries and KMS hostnames.
[11:46] Anya: curious about patching — how do you handle updates to the runtime in an air-gapped environment?
[11:51] Maya: we provide signed release bundles. you import them using the offline installer, verify signatures (we provide public keys to validate), and apply updates during a scheduled maintenance window. we also provide an upgrade checklist and rollback steps.
[12:05] Leah: from a compliance standpoint we need proof that older keys are properly retired and inaccessible after rotation. is that something you support?
[12:12] Maya: yes, key revocation is logged and keys are marked as retired in your KMS/HSM. you can set retention/amnesty windows and we can provide proof-of-destruction artifacts if you require physical HSM key erasure (subject to vendor features).
[12:25] Priya: can you walk briefly through a sample packet flow for an inference request in the air-gapped scenario?
[12:30] Maya: sure: client -> internal proxy -> load balancer -> inference pod (runtime). runtime loads model from local store after verifying signature with HSM-backed public key, performs inference, writes audit event to local audit service which batches and forwards to internal SIEM over mTLS. no external network hops.
[12:49] Jordan: um, I want to note that you can also enable prefix/KV caching policies that keep responses local and reduce egress risk if you do any remote validation.
[13:00] Carlos: what's the recommended approach for debugging issues without enabling sensitive logging?
[13:04] Maya: use sampling and structured traces where you redact payloads. we have a debug mode that captures metadata only and requires a signed approval to capture payloads.
[13:15] Anya: do you support hardware attestation like TPM-based host attestation?
[13:20] Maya: yes, we can integrate with remote attestation for hosts. the runtime can verify TPM quotes during boot and register the host only if it attests correctly. this is useful for lock-down mode.
[13:31] Priya: are there any known limitations with integrating third-party HSMs? vendor specifics maybe?
[13:36] Maya: most vendors supported; differences are in KMIP feature set and RPC ports. vendor drivers might require particular OS kernels. we'll include vendor-specific notes in the doc.
[13:47] Jordan: let's surface a short risk table — Maya, can you call out top 4 risks and mitigations?
[13:52] Maya: sure: 1) egress leakage — mitigated by deny-by-default egress, proxy allow rules, and private peering. 2) key compromise — mitigate using HSM, short-lived certs, and RBAC. 3) unauthorized model access — mitigate via per-model RBAC and signed artifacts. 4) audit gaps — mitigate with agented forwarding to SIEM and signed immutable logs.
[14:17] Tom: thanks. can you provide example firewall rules (ACLs) we can paste into our firewall manager?
[14:23] Maya: yes, we'll provide a starting set with CIDRs, ports (KMIP, HEC, management), and example iptables or pf rules.
[14:31] Priya: one request: we need all security decisions documented in a single SOW appendix for our vendor risk team. can Redwood produce that?
[14:37] Jordan: yes, Jordan will prepare an SOW appendix covering network flows, ports, compliance controls, and the pilot scope.
[14:45] Leah: schedule wise, we're aiming for a pilot in six weeks. is that realistic?
[14:50] Jordan: yes, pilot in six weeks is feasible if we get the egress list and sign the SOW within two weeks.
[14:57] [14:57] Evan: quick note— we'll include a compliance artifact zip in the next email.
[15:01] Carlos: now a few detailed Qs from Priya about HSM connectivity — Priya go ahead.
[15:06] Priya: thanks. my team wonders if we can require mutual-auth and restrict ciphers to NIST-approved sets.
[15:12] Maya: yes, cipher suites are configurable and we can enforce NIST-approved ciphers and TLS 1.3 only. mutual auth is supported via client certs provisioned into the HSM.
[15:23] Priya: and can logs be forwarded over an isolated management network with no route to the internet?
[15:28] Maya: absolutely — use a separate management network with peering only to your SIEM. no internet route required.
[15:33] Tom: question: what happens to long running KV cache when a host is rebooted — any leakage risk?
[15:39] Maya: KV cache is ephemeral; on reboot it's cleared. if you persist caches make sure disk is encrypted and keys are stored in the KMS.
[15:47] Carlos: can we enforce a no-ssh policy on inference hosts and only allow session-manager style access?
[15:53] Jordan: yes, we recommended just-in-time access and disabling persistent SSH. use audit proxies for session recording.
[15:59] Priya: are there any telemetry endpoints that are mandatory to reach Redwood-hosted services?
[16:04] Maya: not mandatory. you can opt-in. for hosted telemetry we push metrics; for Private you can ship metrics to your collector.
[16:12] Leah: question about cross-region replication of logs. do you support encrypted replication to a DR site within EU?
[16:18] Maya: yes, replicate over an encrypted tunnel between sites with keys managed in your HSM. ensure replication endpoints are behind access controls.
[16:26] Jordan: we're at about 16 minutes in; do folks want to deep dive on any one area now?
[16:31] Carlos: let's go deeper on the HSM side for 15 minutes.
[16:34] Maya: ok, HSM deep dive: supported interfaces PKCS#11, KMIP; librariy drivers must be present on the host if PKCS#11. with KMIP you can use a TLS connection to the HSM; certificate provisioning can be automated using your CA.
[16:48] Priya: do you have an example of a KMIP config snippet?
[16:51] Maya: yes, we'll send a sample in the follow up.
[16:54] Tom: how do you handle high availability for the KMS/HSM? we need failover without exposing keys.
[16:59] Maya: recommend an active-passive HSM cluster with private replication; endpoint failover via VIPs, and the runtime should be configured with a prioritized list of HSM endpoints. signed logs help reconcile which HSM served a request.
[17:14] Priya: can we rotate host keys without downtime?
[17:18] Maya: yes with short-lived certs and a rolling rotation agent; you can stage the new certs and then flip traffic. HSM vendor features vary.
[17:28] Carlos: do you support offline key import/export for key custody transfers?
[17:33] Maya: some HSMs support key export wrapped by a transport key; otherwise you do key ceremony with vendor tooling. we can document the process.
[17:43] Jordan: ok, we're roughly at half hour, folks — anything else on HSM?
[17:47] Priya: one more — can we prevent operators from seeing key material in memory?
[17:52] Maya: yes, HSM provides cryptographic operations without exposing private keys; runtime uses only handles and never dumps keys to process memory. use kernel hardening and seccomp to reduce exposure.
[18:05] [18:05] Jordan: let's switch briefly to network ACL examples and then recap.
[18:09] Maya: example ACL: allow tcp 5696 from inference-subnet to hsm-subnet; allow tcp 8081 from loadbalancer to pod-subnet; deny all outbound to 0.0.0.0/0 from inference-subnet; allow egress to internal artifact-registry on port 443.
[18:25] Tom: great, can you share a sample iptables and calico policy in the doc?
[18:29] Maya: yes.
[18:31] Leah: last question — how do we prove time-of-access for audit events? we need tamper-evidence.
[18:36] Evan: we support signed timestamps and append-only logs with HMAC, plus forward to a WORM (write once read many) store if required for compliance.
[18:46] Carlos: ok let's do recap and next steps.
[18:49] Jordan: recap: 1) Redwood provides multiple KMS/HSM integration patterns including PKCS#11 and KMIP, sidecar and broker modes. 2) egress must be deny-by-default, with explicit exceptions for HSM and SIEM. 3) logs can be signed and forwarded to Splunk HEC and stored in WORM as needed. 4) RBAC/SSO maps to per-model permissions and supports SAML/LDAP. 5) air-gapped model signing supported.
[19:14] Jordan: next steps captured: Maya to send KMS integration guide and network diagrams by 2026-05-19; Jordan to draft SOW appendix and cost sketch by 2026-05-20; Carlos to share egress/allow-list by 2026-05-22 and team to schedule rack walkthrough week of 2026-05-25.
[19:32] Leah: thanks, that's helpful. we'll review and follow up with any clarifying Qs.
[19:37] Carlos: thanks everyone.
[19:39] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up via email with the artifact bundle.
[19:42] [19:42] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: filler words and slight mis-attributions may be present; some technical terms spelled out differently in the transcript (e.g., KMIP, PKCS11 as PKCS#11 or PK C S).
